title: Auditability: Immutable Logs and Evidence Bundles

questions.question: Risk decisions are stored in a database table that the application can UPDATE, with an updated_at column. An examiner asks you to prove a row was not changed after a backfill. What can the table alone show?
options: That the row was not changed, as long as updated_at is older than the backfill date
That the row was not changed, provided the nightly backup contains the identical row
Nothing conclusive: anyone who could edit the row could also edit updated_at and backups
That the row was not changed, because the database transaction log records every write
questions.explanation: A mutable record is a claim whose credibility equals that of everyone who can edit it; the backfill itself set updated_at, and backups are equally mutable and unverifiable by the examiner. The database's write-ahead log is the strongest distractor, but it is retained briefly, controlled by the same operator, and not designed to be shown to a third party as proof.

questions.question: An operator edits entry #3 of a hash-chained log, recomputes its hash, then rewrites #4 through #8 with new prev pointers and hashes. With no checkpoints, what does a chain verifier report?
options: A hash mismatch at entry #3, because its content no longer matches the original
A broken link between #3 and #4, because #4 still points to the old hash of #3
A sequence gap, because rewritten entries receive new sequence numbers from the log
Nothing: every hash matches its content and every link matches its predecessor
questions.explanation: A hash chain proves internal consistency, not that this is the chain that existed yesterday. After a full suffix rewrite every check passes. The broken-link distractor is what happens if the operator stops after rehashing #3; rewriting the suffix removes it. Detecting this needs an anchor held by someone else, such as a signed checkpoint of the Merkle root.

questions.question: Why does RFC 6962 hash leaves as SHA-256(0x00 || data) and interior nodes as SHA-256(0x01 || left || right)?
options: So an interior node's two child hashes can never be passed off as a leaf in a proof
So that leaf hashes and node hashes sort apart, making the tree faster to search
So the tree stays balanced when the number of leaves is not a power of two
So that a SHA-256 collision in one leaf cannot propagate to the root of the tree
questions.explanation: Without domain separation, the 64 bytes of two child hashes could be presented as leaf data, letting an attacker prove inclusion of a fake leaf (a second-preimage attack on the tree). Balancing comes from splitting at the largest power of two below n, not from the prefix, and a real SHA-256 collision would break the scheme regardless.

questions.question: Checkpoint 1 covering entries 0..4 was signed by the time-stamp authority at 10:01. Checkpoint 2 covering 0..8 was signed at 10:08. Entry #6 says 10:02. What is actually proven about when #6 was written?
options: It was written at exactly 10:02, because its timestamp is covered by the signed root
It was written after 10:01 and no later than 10:08, the window between the two seals
It was written no later than 10:01, because it follows entries sealed in checkpoint 1
Nothing about its time is proven, because its timestamp came from the operator's clock
questions.explanation: The TSA's signatures bound existence: #6 was not in the 5-entry log sealed at 10:01 and was in the 9-entry log sealed at 10:08. Its own 10:02 timestamp is only the operator's claim within that window. 'Nothing is proven' is the strongest distractor: the entry's own clock proves nothing, but the seals do, which is why the seal interval is the backdating window.

questions.question: A regulator investigating one complaint needs to verify that customer's two decisions without seeing anyone else's. What should the evidence bundle contain?
options: A database dump of the full log, plus the TSA-signed checkpoint covering every entry
The two entries as JSON, with each entry's own hash and the log operator's signature
The two entries, plus the hash of every other entry so the root can be recomputed
The two entries as canonical bytes, their audit paths, and the TSA-signed checkpoint
questions.explanation: Canonical bytes let the verifier recompute exactly what was hashed; O(log n) audit paths prove inclusion in the signed root without revealing other entries; the TSA signature makes the root trustworthy independent of the operator. A full dump or every other hash discloses far more than needed or scales linearly, and an operator's own signature proves nothing about rewrites by that operator.

questions.question: Your verifier passes on every bundle. A customer says a decline was never logged at all. What does the verifier prove about that claim?
options: Nothing: logs prove what was written, so omission needs log-before-act plus reconciliation
That the claim is false, because a missing decision would break the hash chain at that point
That the claim is false, because the Merkle root commits to every decision the engine made
That the claim is true, because the bundle has no entry for that payment's identifier
questions.explanation: A tamper-evident log proves the integrity of what was appended; a decision that was never appended leaves no gap in the chain or the tree. The control is process: append the decision before returning it, and reconcile every authorization in the ledger against a log entry. The chain-gap distractor confuses deleting an appended entry, which is detected, with never appending one.
